question_text: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of a prolonged course of diarrhea. He reports that he has had 3–4 large volume watery stools daily for the last several weeks. He has no pain with bowel movements, no abdominal pain, and no blood in his stools. He is homeless and uses recreational drugs. He also reports that he usually drinks a half-liter of whiskey, or whatever else he can find, every day and he has done this for several years. The physical exam is notable for a hyperpigmented rash across his face, neck, chest, and the backs of his hands and forearms. On mental status exam, he is oriented to person and place but not time; he scores a 23/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA). This patient's presentation is most likely related to which of the following micronutrients?

                    ### Question
                    A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of a prolonged course of diarrhea. He reports that he has had 3–4 large volume watery stools daily for the last several weeks. He has no pain with bowel movements, no abdominal pain, and no blood in his stools. He is homeless and uses recreational drugs. He also reports that he usually drinks a half-liter of whiskey, or whatever else he can find, every day and he has done this for several years. The physical exam is notable for a hyperpigmented rash across his face, neck, chest, and the backs of his hands and forearms. On mental status exam, he is oriented to person and place but not time; he scores a 23/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA). This patient's presentation is most likely related to which of the following micronutrients?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms of prolonged diarrhea, hyperpigmented rash, and cognitive impairment, combined with his history of homelessness and chronic alcohol use, strongly suggest a deficiency in niacin (Vitamin B3), leading to pellagra. Pellagra is characterized by the 'three Ds': dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, which align with the patient's presentation. The evidence path confirming niacin's role in causing pellagra supports this diagnosis. Other vitamin deficiencies, such as Vitamin B12, Vitamin C, Vitamin D, and Vitamin B2, are less likely to cause the observed combination of symptoms. Vitamin B12 deficiency primarily presents with neurological symptoms and anemia but not typically diarrhea or rash. Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy, marked by symptoms like bleeding gums and bruising, rather than diarrhea or a hyperpigmented rash. Vitamin D deficiency is mainly associated with bone issues, and Vitamin B2 deficiency might cause skin lesions and sore throat but is less commonly linked to severe diarrhea or cognitive impairment.
